readerTitle: Why the ATM gives your card back first
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (ATM, 전자레인지) + 일화 (신고 시게오의 스프링 접시) + 가상 사례 (유통 창고, 재무팀)
insight: 실수는 사람을 더 조심하게 만들어서가 아니라, 실수가 일어날 수 없거나 즉시 드러나도록 일의 구조를 바꿔서 줄인다.
misconception: 실수는 부주의 때문이니 교육하고 주의를 주고 검수자를 늘리면 해결된다.

sources.text: Shingo, S. (1986). Zero Quality Control: Source Inspection and the Poka-yoke System. Productivity Press.
ATM 카드 반환 순서, 전자레인지 문 잠금 장치는 일반적인 제품 설계 관찰
창고와 재무팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '많은 ATM이 현금보다 카드를 먼저 돌려준다'는 널리 알려진 설계 사례지만 나라와 기종마다 다릅니다. 카드에 'many cash machines'로만 썼습니다.
스위치 조립 작업자가 스프링을 빠뜨리자 신고 시게오가 스프링을 먼저 접시에 담게 했다는 이야기는 여러 자료에 전해지지만 세부 내용은 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에 일화로 표시했습니다.
'baka-yoke(바보 방지)'에서 'poka-yoke(부주의 실수 방지)'로 이름을 바꾼 경위는 Shingo 관련 자료로 확인하세요.
창고 오피킹, 재무팀 중복 지급 사례에는 실제 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. 모두 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Why the ATM gives your card back first
body: At many cash machines, you take your card back before the cash comes out. It feels like a small detail.
It's a fix for a very common mistake. People came for cash. Once they had it, they walked away and left the card behind. So the machine stopped trusting memory and changed the order.

image.label: A hand taking a card from an ATM while cash waits
image.brief: 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. ATM 화면 앞에서 손이 카드를 먼저 뽑고, 현금 투입구에는 지폐가 아직 대기 중. 카드 쪽에 '1', 현금 쪽에 '2' 숫자 표시. 실제 은행 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Two shampoos, one wrong box.
body: You run a distribution warehouse for a beauty retailer. Two shampoo sizes sit side by side and look almost the same. Pickers keep grabbing the wrong one, and stores complain every week.
What do you do first?

options.text: Retrain pickers and put up a sign: "Check the size!"
options.feedback: Cheap and quick, but it asks tired people to be more careful forever. Signs fade into the background within weeks.

options.text: Add a checker who inspects every box before it ships
options.feedback: You catch most errors before stores see them. But you pay for a second person, and the mistake still happens. Checkers get tired too.

options.text: Move the sizes apart and require a scan that beeps and stops if the wrong item goes in
options.feedback: The wrong pick is caught at the moment it happens, with no extra person. It costs some setup, and it only works if scanning stays mandatory.

cards.title: A dish of springs.
body: A story often told about the Japanese engineer **Shigeo Shingo**, details vary by source: workers assembling a switch sometimes forgot one of its two small springs.
Reminders didn't help. So Shingo had them place both springs in a small dish before starting. If a spring was left in the dish at the end, the mistake was obvious on the spot.
Nobody became more careful. The step itself changed.

cards.title: Mistake-proofing
body: **Mistake-proofing** means designing a task so the error can't happen, or is caught the instant it does. Shingo called it *poka-yoke*, Japanese for avoiding inadvertent mistakes.

There are two strengths. **Prevent:** the wrong action is impossible, like a microwave that stops when the door opens. **Detect:** the wrong action triggers an alert right away, like the leftover spring or the scanner's beep.
Prevention is stronger. Detection is often cheaper.

image.label: Two panels: a shape that won't fit, and a warning light
image.brief: 두 칸 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Prevent': 네모 블록이 둥근 구멍에 안 들어가는 모습. 오른쪽 'Detect': 접시에 남은 스프링 하나와 깜빡이는 경고등. 간결한 선 스타일, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four ways to build it in.
body: Most mistake-proofing uses one of a few simple moves:
list: **Shape:** parts or tools only fit the right way
**Order:** the next step won't start until the risky one is done, like card before cash
**Count:** a set number of items is laid out, so a gap shows
**Stop:** the process halts when something is off, instead of carrying on
cards.callout: The best fixes are cheap, built into the work, and need no one to remember anything.

cards.title: It's everywhere once you look.
body: A restaurant uses a different-colored board for raw meat, so it never touches salad. A pharmacy shelves look-alike drug names apart. A shop's till won't close the sale until the age check is entered.
In each case, the business stopped asking "Who made the mistake?" and asked "Why was the mistake so easy to make?"
cards.softwareNote: A form that won't submit without a valid date, or a tool that makes you type a project's name before deleting it, is mistake-proofing. The product blocks the slip instead of apologizing afterward.

cards.title: Not every guard holds.
body: Warnings that fire too often get ignored. If a scanner beeps at half the right picks, people learn to tap past it.
Guards that slow the work invite workarounds. Staff tape down the switch or skip the scan when the rush hits.
And mistake-proofing costs money to set up. Spend it on errors that are frequent or expensive, not on every possible slip.

cards.title: Now it's a finance team.
body: You lead accounts payable inside a large company. Twice this year, a supplier invoice was paid twice. Once, money went to a fraudster's new bank account after a fake email.
Which fix fits the idea best?

options.text: Email the team a reminder to double-check every payment
options.feedback: It costs nothing, but it relies on memory and attention, the exact things that failed. The next busy month brings the same errors.

options.text: Have a second person approve every payment
options.feedback: It catches some errors, but it doubles the workload and reviewers start approving on autopilot. The duplicate is still easy to create.

options.text: Have the system block a repeat invoice number for the same supplier, and hold any bank-detail change until someone calls the supplier on a known number
options.feedback: Duplicates become impossible and bank changes get a built-in stop. It takes setup time, and the callback must never be skipped.

cards.title: Fix the step, not the person.
body: When a mistake repeats, don't ask people to try harder. Change the work so the mistake can't happen, or shows up the instant it does.
**Try it today:** name one error that happened twice this month. Ask which move would stop it: shape, order, count or stop.
